From Community to Catastrophe: Mapping Jewish Life and the Holocaust in Monor

A map of Jewish Monor reconstructs the institutions, homes and everyday spaces of a once-thriving community before the deportations of 1944. Places now encountered as ordinary streets are read as historical evidence.

Borbala KlacsmannStoryMapWho Owns Memory? · 2026

Encounter the story

History through places, objects and voices

In 1862, 25 families established the Jewish community of Monor. This prosperous congregation had their own synagogue and institutions, while the local Jews played an active role in the town’s economic and social life. However, the anti-Jewish persecution put an abrupt and tragic end to the coexistence of Jews and non-Jews: the Jews were forced to move into designated houses, then they were taken to the local brick factory which served as a collection site for 9,000 Jews from Monor and the surrounding areas. The victims were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau in three trains on 6 and 8 July 1944.

The chapters below bring the contributor’s sources and images into a readable, illustrated public-history narrative. Photographs and visual records can be enlarged by selecting them.

Where did Jewish communal life take place, and what remains visible in the town today?

The original work

This is an original visual from the participant’s submitted work. It provides a point of entry to the project’s historical argument and digital form.

Chapter 01

A community within the town

In 1862, 25 families established Monor’s Jewish community. Over time, a synagogue, communal institutions, workplaces and homes became part of the town’s everyday urban life.

Chapter 02

From persecution to deportation

Anti-Jewish persecution violently changed the geography of the town in 1944. Designated houses and the brick factory became spaces of confinement before deportations to Auschwitz-Birkenau.

Chapter 03

The map as a public-history method

By identifying the locations of former institutions and homes, the project asks visitors to see streets and buildings as evidence of the lives that once shaped Monor.
